zh-CN.title: 如何使用 · 等高线地形图

lines: 第 1 步：顶部选一种地形（山地 / 盆地 / 丘陵 / 高原 / 平原），画面会换成对应的等高线图。
第 2 步：把鼠标移到图上任意位置，底部会显示该点的海拔、相对高度和地形部位。
第 3 步：观察左边的立体地形与右边的等高线图，找出同一个山峰，看它在两张图上分别长什么样。
第 4 步：点右下角「取消上色」，只留等高线；再点一次恢复分层设色，对比哪种更便于判读。
第 5 步：对着右侧的判读要点，依次在图上找出一个山峰、一条山脊、一条山谷、一处鞍部和一处陡崖。
在地图上，把海拔相同的点用线连起来，这条线就叫等高线。
相邻两条等高线之间的高差叫等高距：本图山地、高原、盆地用 100 米，丘陵用 10 米，平原用 5 米。
等高线的闭合圈，数值由中心向四周递减的是山峰；四周高中间低的是盆地。
等高线向海拔低处凸出的是山脊（分水线）；向海拔高处凸出的是山谷（集水线）。
两个山峰之间低下去的地方叫鞍部；等高线重叠或挤成一团的地方是陡崖。
等高线越密，坡度越陡；越疏，坡度越缓。
每 5 条等高线加粗一条叫计曲线，上面标着海拔，方便读数。
海拔：地面某一点高出海平面的垂直距离。
相对高度：两个地点海拔的差值，也就是图上两点的落差。
底部读数里的「相对高度」是本图最低点到该点的高差。

sections.h: 五种地体的等高线特征
lines: 山地：海拔高、起伏大，等高线密集且数值跨度大。
盆地：四周高、中间低，等高线由外向内数值递减，常有河流发育。
丘陵：海拔不高、坡度和缓，等高线稀疏弯曲。
高原：海拔高而顶面平坦，等高线中部稀疏、边缘密集。
平原：海拔低、地面平坦，等高线很少甚至没有。
分层设色：按固定高程档位套固定色阶（深绿→浅绿→绿→浅黄→黄→浅褐→褐→白），同一档内颜色完全相同。
山峰用 ▲ 加高程数字标注。
河流用蓝色线表示，沿谷底（等高线凸向高处的一侧）流。
陡崖用红色锯齿线表示。
指北针在图幅右上角，比例尺在左下角，分层设色图例在右下角。
地形剖面图在图幅底部：沿南北中线剖开地面，标出各点海拔，看清起伏。
把「等高线密集 = 陡」记反：密集是陡，稀疏是缓。
把山脊和山谷看反：看凸出的方向 —— 凸向低处是山脊，凸向高处是山谷。
忽视等高距：等高距变了，同样的等高线密度代表的坡度就不同。
把计曲线当成普通等高线：计曲线加粗并标了数值，读高程要看它。
Step 1: pick a terrain type at the top (mountains / basin / hills / plateau / plain) — the map switches to its contour map.
Step 2: move the pointer anywhere on the map; the footer shows elevation, relative height and the terrain feature.
Step 3: compare the 3D block on the left with the contour map on the right — find the same peak in both.
Step 4: click “No colour” at the bottom right to keep only the contour lines; click again to restore the colour fill.
Step 5: using the panel on the right, find one peak, one ridge, one valley, one saddle and one cliff.
Connect points of equal elevation on a map and you get a contour line.
The height gap between neighbouring contours is the contour interval: 100 m for mountains, plateau and basin; 10 m for hills; 5 m for plain.
A closed loop whose values decrease outward is a peak; high ground around a low centre is a basin.
Contours bulging toward lower ground form a ridge (watershed); bulging toward higher ground form a valley (drainage).
The low ground between two peaks is a saddle; overlapping or tightly crowded contours mark a cliff.
The closer the contours, the steeper the slope; the wider apart, the gentler.
Every 5th contour is bolded as an index contour and labelled with its elevation.
Elevation is the vertical height of a point above sea level.
Relative height is the difference between two elevations — the drop between two points on the map.
The relative height in the footer is measured from the lowest point of this map.

sections.h: Contour patterns of the five terrains
lines: Mountains: high elevation, large relief, dense contours over a wide value range.
Basin: high rim, low centre; values decrease inward, often with a river.
Hills: low elevation, gentle slopes, sparse winding contours.
Plateau: high but flat on top — contours sparse in the middle and crowded at the edges.
Plain: low and flat — few or no contour lines at all.
Hypsometric tint: fixed colour bands by elevation (dark green → light green → green → pale yellow → yellow → light brown → brown → white); each band is a flat colour.
Peaks are marked with a ▲ and their elevation.
Rivers are drawn in blue along the valley floor (where contours bulge uphill).
Cliffs are marked with a red saw-tooth line.
A north arrow sits top-right, a scale bar bottom-left, and the tint legend bottom-right.
The terrain profile along the bottom cuts the ground open and labels elevations, showing the relief at a glance.
Reversing dense and sparse: dense means steep, sparse means gentle.
Mixing up ridge and valley — look which way the bulge points: toward lower ground is a ridge, toward higher ground is a valley.
Ignoring the contour interval: change it and the same spacing means a different slope.
Treating index contours as ordinary ones — they are bold and labelled, so read elevations off them.
